solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Sweet dance with bachelor

blocks.note: a Latin American ballroom dance
Bachelor of Arts, the basic university degree

explanation.surface: A dessert eaten during a dance with an unmarried man.
explanation.walkthrough: The dance swallows the first part of the answer and the degree finishes it; the word break falls inside the dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A rum baba is a small yeasted cake soaked in rum syrup, served as a pudding or dessert.

clue.text: Back in Montecito, bored stiff

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows, spanning the comma
going back means reading from right to left instead of the usual direction

blocks.note: the tail of the town name joined to the start of the next word

explanation.surface: Someone back in the Californian town of Montecito finds life there tediously dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bored stiff' reads as one idiom, but it splits: 'bored' supplies letters and 'stiff' alone is the definition. Montecito is a wealthy town near Santa Barbara.
explanation.definitionFit: Movements described as robotic are mechanical and rigid, lacking natural human ease.

clue.text: Element of broadcast amusing me

indicators.note: seed that is broadcast is scattered widely, so the letters get thrown about

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Part of a radio or TV programme happens to entertain the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Element of broadcast' sounds like a segment of a programme; 'Element' is really the chemical kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnesium is a chemical element, the light silvery metal with atomic number twelve.

clue.text: Bubbly roommate’s first out of bed

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word is wanted

blocks.note: Asti is a sparkling Italian wine
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cheerful flatmate is the first one up in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bubbly' looks like an adjective for the roommate's personality, but it is a noun meaning sparkling wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Astir means up and about, awake and moving, the opposite of still lying asleep.

clue.text: Army’s leader thumped half-cut ally with embarrassment

indicators.note: the leader of a group is the one at the front, so the opening letter
cutting off half of a word throws away half its letters

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
to bash is to hit hard
the second half of this four-letter word

explanation.surface: A commanding officer, ashamed, hit a drunken friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for tipsy, which colours the surface; here it means keep only half of the following word.
explanation.definitionFit: To act abashedly is to behave in a shamefaced, self-conscious way, which is how embarrassment shows.

clue.text: Report revolutionary system in Leo’s office

indicators.note: a revolution turns a thing round, so the word is turned back to front

blocks.note: a report can be a bang, the sound of a gun going off
a mode is a method or way of operating

explanation.surface: A news account of a radical new arrangement inside the office of somebody called Leo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' suggests a written document, but it is the noise of a shot. Leo here is any of the thirteen popes of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Popedom is the office or tenure of a pope, a role held by several pontiffs named Leo.

clue.text: Upset about drivel in essay

indicators.note: something upset in a down clue is turned over, so the word reads bottom to top

blocks.note: pap is worthless, trivial talk or writing
re is Latin for concerning or on the subject of

explanation.surface: Someone is annoyed at the nonsense written in a student's composition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like the angry reader, but it acts only on the short word for 'about'; 'in' just links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper is a written academic piece or dissertation, the same thing as an essay.

clue.text: Secretaries in City University, side by side

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the French capital
standard abbreviation
personal assistants, abbreviated, in the plural

explanation.surface: Office secretaries at a London university work next to each other.
explanation.walkthrough: City University is a real London institution, which hides the split into a capital city plus U. The assistants go between the I and the S of the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Pari passu is a Latin phrase meaning equally and simultaneously, at an equal pace, hence alongside one another.

clue.text: Prevent cleaner scrubbing chap

indicators.note: to scrub something is to cancel or erase it, so letters are wiped out

blocks.note: a cleaning agent for washing
a gent is a man, a fellow

explanation.surface: Stop the cleaning lady from scrubbing a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrubbing' fits a cleaner so naturally that it hides its job of removal. The man is taken off the end of the washing product.
explanation.definitionFit: To deter is to discourage or hinder someone from acting, so it can stop an action happening.

clue.text: Card index regularly covered by manuscripts in chaos

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals means every second letter
a thing covered by another is wrapped inside it

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for manuscripts
the even-numbered letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A library card index buried under heaps of manuscripts in a disorderly mess.
explanation.walkthrough: The selected letters go between the M and the SS of the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Madness can mean wild confusion or turmoil, as in 'it was madness in there', so it fits disorder.

clue.text: Sound from great height

blocks.note: great in size
standard abbreviation for height

explanation.surface: A noise heard from a lofty position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' is the stretch of water, not a noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A bight is a wide curving bay or inlet of the sea, and a sound is likewise a sea inlet or channel.

clue.text: Perhaps made it into hit parade — it’s fantastic!

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful and unreal, so the letters take on a fanciful new form

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the dash and apostrophe

explanation.surface: Excitement that a song may have reached the singles chart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit parade' is the music chart, but the phrase splits: 'it into hit' describes adding an H sound. 'Perhaps' flags this as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspirate a sound is to pronounce it with a breath of H, which is what turns the word 'it' into 'hit'.

clue.text: Stars in interminable BBC soap

indicators.note: without a terminus, that is with no end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: the long-running BBC radio drama about a farming family

explanation.surface: Celebrities appear in a never-ending British serial drama.
explanation.walkthrough: The Archers is a BBC radio soap opera that has run since 1951, so 'interminable' doubles as a joke about its length. 'Stars' are celebrities in the surface but a constellation here.
explanation.definitionFit: The Archer is Sagittarius, a zodiac constellation, so it is a pattern of stars in the sky.

clue.text: Released from trap, old men verbally break down

indicators.note: trap is slang for mouth, and what comes out of the mouth is spoken

blocks.note: an old man is a father, and pa is a father, so the plural is pas

explanation.surface: Elderly men freed from a snare collapse in a fit of talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' is informal for father; in a British accent 'pa's' and the answer sound alike. 'Released from trap' reads like an escape, but trap is slang for mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: To parse a sentence is to analyse it grammatically, splitting the words into their parts and roles.

clue.text: Caught fish? Hold on tight!

blocks.note: cricket scoring abbreviation for caught
a ling is a long, cod-like sea fish

explanation.surface: An angler who has hooked a fish is urged to keep a firm grip.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket scorecards C stands for caught, a convention setters borrow freely.
explanation.definitionFit: To cling is to grip firmly and not let go, so the instruction to grasp tightly matches the verb.

clue.text: Excitedly greet aged technophile

indicators.note: excited things are agitated and jumbled, so the letters are stirred about

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Warmly welcoming an elderly lover of new technology.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs old age with a love of tech for the contrast; the definition is the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: A gadgeteer is someone who delights in gadgets and devices, just as a technophile is enthusiastic about technology.

clue.text: Powerful families of decidedly vacuous, unpleasant people

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the inside is cleared out and only the outer letters stay

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
nasties are horrible people or things

explanation.surface: Ruling clans made up of thoroughly empty-headed, horrible people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decidedly vacuous' reads as 'very empty-headed', but 'vacuous' empties the adverb itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A dynasty is a line of rulers or an influential family whose power passes down the generations.

clue.text: Sat in gaol, suffering homesickness

indicators.note: something suffering is in a bad way, damaged and knocked out of shape

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A prisoner in his cell pines for home.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaol is the British spelling of jail, and its letters are needed exactly as spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: Nostalgia originally meant acute longing for one's home, from Greek nostos, return, and algos, pain.

clue.text: Intriguing old American jokers

blocks.note: a member of the ancient Andean civilisation of Peru
a hoot is a very funny person

explanation.surface: Fascinating pranksters from an earlier era in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old American' suggests a past US citizen, but it is an ancient South American people. 'Intriguing' means plotting, not fascinating.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in cahoots means conspiring together in secret, and to intrigue is to scheme or plot covertly.

clue.text: Noah’s son with a thirsty and extremely audacious baboon

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so the outside letters

blocks.note: Ham was one of Noah's three sons in Genesis
taken as written
in need of a drink
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: One of the Ark's family accompanied by a parched and very bold monkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely audacious' reads as 'very bold', but it asks for the ends of the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The hamadryas is the sacred baboon of north-east Africa and Arabia, revered in ancient Egypt.

clue.text: Shot and injured, left with journalist

blocks.note: wounded
standard abbreviation
ED, an editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter is left wounded after a shooting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot and injured' reads as a gunshot wound, but 'Shot' stands alone as the definition in its sense of moved fast.
explanation.definitionFit: To shoot along or past is to move very swiftly, and to hurtle is to rush at great speed.

clue.text: Public fears oddly invisible threat to health

indicators.note: doing something oddly here means skipping alternate letters, keeping one in two

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: People are strangely worried about an unseen danger to their wellbeing, like a virus.
explanation.walkthrough: Here 'oddly' keeps the even letters, an accepted looseness; the odd ones spell nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: An ulcer is a sore that typically forms inside the stomach, out of sight, and harms the body.

clue.text: Eggs on clergyman in girls’ school

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing on another sits above it, so it comes first

blocks.note: fish eggs
a senior priest in charge of a cathedral

explanation.surface: A cleric is pelted with eggs at a girls' school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eggs on' looks like the phrasal verb meaning urges, but it is fish eggs placed on top of the cleric.
explanation.definitionFit: Roedean is a famous independent boarding school for girls on the Sussex coast near Brighton in England.

clue.text: Shooter in Moroccan mountains with the French

blocks.note: the Rif is a mountain range in northern Morocco
the masculine French word for the

explanation.surface: A sniper hides in the Atlas region accompanied by French troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shooter' suggests a person, but it is the gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A shooter is informal slang for a gun, and a rifle is a long-barrelled firearm.

clue.text: Female isn’t commonly feeble

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
ain't is the colloquial, non-standard form

explanation.surface: A woman is generally not weak, contradicting a stereotype.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonly' looks like 'usually', but it marks a vulgar or dialect form of the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A faint sound, light or effort is weak and lacking strength, so it is feeble.

clue.text: It helps you stop, pause and drive away as stated

indicators.note: what is stated is said out loud, so the sound counts and not the spelling

blocks.note: a break is a pause or rest
to shoo is to chase off an animal or person

explanation.surface: Advice on how to take a rest when tired of driving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive away' suggests setting off in a car, which fits the motoring picture, but it means chase off.
explanation.definitionFit: A brake shoe is the curved block that presses against a wheel or drum to slow a vehicle down.

clue.text: Topless snog behind British Library is heaven

indicators.note: with its top removed, a word in a down clue loses its first letter
one piece placed behind another comes after it

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for the national library in London
snog is British slang for a passionate kiss

explanation.surface: A shirtless kiss out behind the British Library feels like paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' suggests bare skin but only removes a letter. A snog is British slang for a long kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: Bliss is perfect happiness, the sort of joy described as heaven, as in 'it was heaven'.

clue.text: Fungus thus beginning to thrive

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: Latin for therefore
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A mould is therefore starting to flourish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to thrive' reads as a phrase about growth, which suits a fungus, but it just wants an initial.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergot is a fungal disease of rye and other cereals, caused by a Claviceps species.

clue.text: Angry lion and tiger mooching about

indicators.note: an angry creature is wild and stirred up, so the letters thrash about

blocks.note: taken as written, the joining word ignored

explanation.surface: Two irritable big cats prowl around restlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' sits inside the fodder as a joiner and gives no letters. To mooch is British slang for to hang about aimlessly.
explanation.definitionFit: Loitering means lingering idly without purpose, and mooching about is wandering around with nothing to do.

clue.text: Fondle backside of good-looking guy?

indicators.note: a backside is the rear, so the last letter of the word

blocks.note: the final letter of the hyphenated word
a guy is a rope holding a tent or mast steady

explanation.surface: Someone is tempted to touch the bottom of a handsome man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backside' makes it sound as if the bottom is being fondled, but it only selects a letter. 'Guy' is a guy rope, not a man.
explanation.definitionFit: To grope is to touch someone sexually in a clumsy, unwanted way, a crude kind of caressing.

clue.text: Toads jumping across road confused old folk

indicators.note: jumping things leap about, so the letters land in a new order
lying across something means spanning it, so one piece goes either side of the other

blocks.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Muddled elderly people see toads hopping across the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The shuffled amphibians are split around the road abbreviation, which goes between the A and the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A dotard is an old person whose mind has weakened with age, someone in their dotage.

clue.text: Crafty sort of guerrilla hiding face

indicators.note: hiding its face means the front is concealed, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: a partisan is an irregular resistance fighter

explanation.surface: A cunning type of irregular fighter keeps their face masked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crafty' suggests cunning, but here it means skilled in a craft.
explanation.definitionFit: An artisan is a skilled manual worker who makes things by hand, literally a person of craft.
